data.description:
Session One. 

Wordcraft: Optimising writing for publication

This session will consist of two main elements:

1. All the World’s a Stage: Academic Writing for an International Audience

2. Mad About Methods: Writing a Well-Crafted Methods Section

Aim: To equip participants with some of the skills and knowledge needed to successfully publish research in palliative care journals.

Learning objectives:

  1. Learning how to write for a global audience by using clear, accessible language and framing research in a broadly relevant context;
  2. Developing the ability to construct transparent and rigorous methods and ethics sections aligned with reporting standards.

By the end of this interactive session, participants will be better prepared to navigate the publication process and enhance the clarity, credibility, and impact of their palliative care research.

This session brings together three editors from the EAPC journals: Catherine Walshe and Sandra Martins Pereira from Palliative Medicine, and Christopher Jones from the Journal of Palliative Medicine. Together, they will share all you ever wanted to know about how to get your work published. Two interlinked and interactive sessions (this session today, and a second session tomorrow) will focus on some of the most important aspects to ensure your work goes out for peer review (writing for your international audience and persuading the reader of the robustness of your methods and ethics procedures), and then, tomorrow, how to respond appropriately to the peer review comments. If you have ever wanted to really understand how editors make their decisions on your research papers – these are the sessions for you.

data.description:
Panel 5: Optimising Networks: From networks of expertise (NoEs) and clusters into future ways of working and collaborating

Networks of Expertise (NoEs) generate valuable evidence, tools, and collaborations in palliative care, but translating these outputs into enduring change remains a challenge. This panel will explore how network findings can move beyond publications to shape routine practice, policy, training, and ongoing professional collaboration. Panellists will discuss what elements should be sustained after NoEs conclude, and how professional organisations such as the EAPC can lead efforts to standardise approaches, support scale-up, and embed network outputs into everyday palliative care practice across Europe.

Panellists: Stein Kaasa ( JANE2), Cinzia Brunelli (EUonQOL and QOL Cluster), Carlos Centeno (EAPC Atlas), Erna Michiels (Hope4Kids), Phil Larkin (CODE-YAA)

TS: Innovative methods for implementation of digital tools in palliative care: insights from the 4D-PICTURE project
data.description:
Research into the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital tools in Palliative Care.

Increasingly, digital tools are developed to enhance the quality, accessibility, and coordination of care for persons with serious, life-limiting illnesses. While some tools are promising, few (less than 15%!) are sustainably adopted in practice. Key reasons are that such tools: a) lack a system approach, b) lack decent stakeholder collaboration; and c) are insufficiently integrated in complex, diverse care paths. In the seven-country EU/UKRI funded 4D PICTURE project (2022-2027), we design, evaluate and implement digital decision-support tools in oncology and palliative care, and develop innovative methods to improve their implementation (https://4dpicture.eu/). This transdisciplinary project spans palliative care, public health, design, implementation science and many more disciplines. In this theme session, we demonstrate our ongoing work, and use prognostic tools and communication tools as case studies. We provide recommendations for the applicability of the three methods in diverse European palliative care settings.
Introduction: Judith Rietjens, professor Design for Public Health.

Aims and learning objectives:

To demonstrate three promising methods to improve the implementation of digital tools in palliative care:

1. The digital NASSS implementation framework, to analyse the complexity of digital tools in seven domains and provide solution pathways to improve them;

2. The Remote Participatory Bodystorming method, to gather stakeholder feedback on digital tools throughout their developmental process;

3. The service design method MetroMapping, to visualise and redesign care paths to allow seamless integration of digital tools.

After the session, participants have a clear understanding of the three methods. They leave with hands-on inspiration on how to use them across diverse palliative care settings.

data.title: EAPC Partnered Research
data.description:
Panel 6: Engaging with policy

This panel will explore how research consortia can strategically engage policymakers at EU, national and regional levels through timely evidence synthesis, policy briefs, stakeholder alliances, and alignment with legislative and funding cycles. The session will highlight practical approaches to ensure palliative care evidence informs sustainable policy development across Europe.

Panellists: Nancy Preston (Pal-Cycles, EU PAL-COPD and PalSed), Tadeusz Hawrot (PsyPal), Tania Pastrana (RAPHAEL)

Panel 7: The Future of EU Funding Calls:

This panel will examine the new EU health research funding landscape, including mission-oriented approaches, public–private partnerships, widening participation mechanisms, and increasing emphasis on digital transformation, resilience, and implementation impact. The session will explore how the palliative care community can strategically position itself within future EU agendas to secure sustainable investment and strengthen its contribution to European health policy and systems innovation.

Panellists: Andreja  (RAPHAEL), Cinzia Brunelli (EUonQOL), Dirk Hadrich (EU Cancer Mission)

data.title: EAPC Groups: Global Caregiving in Focus: An Interactive Session to Guide Research, Health Systems, and Policy
data.description:
Designed to foster dialogue and collaboration, this interactive session hosted by the EAPC Reference Group for Family Caregiving aims to advance and prioritise the international research and policy agenda for family caregiving. Prof Gardiner will provide an overview of emerging concepts in family caregiver research and present updates from the EAPC White Paper for Family Caregiving. Interactive ranking tools will be used to solicit audience input on emerging research priorities. Prof Hudson will outline progress on the proposed Lancet Commission on family caregiving, which will provide global strategies to improve the well-being of family carers. Interactive tools will be used to collate audience views on policy solutions and effective interventions to contribute to the Commission. Prof De Vleminck will provide an update on emerging interventions and technology innovations supporting family caregiving. A global perspective will provide a ‘state of the science’ and a novel perspective on harnessing technology to support carers.

The aims and learning objectives:
The aim of this interactive session is to provide an overview of new and emerging innovations in family caregiving and engage delegates in identifying priorities for advancing this field of research. The learning objectives are to:
1. Educate attendees on new and emerging concepts and innovations in family caregiving, including global policy, technology innovations and research approaches.
2. Facilitate audience engagement to actively co-produce ranked research priorities and capture stakeholder views to inform health policy and practice.

Speakers: 

Prof Clare Gardiner, Professor of Palliative Care, UK 
Prof Peter Hudson, Director Centre for Palliative Care c/o St Vincent’s Hospital and The University of Melbourne ,Australia
Prof Aline De Vleminck, Associate Professor at the End-of-life Care Research Group, Free University of Brussels (VUB) and Ghent University, Belgium

All speakers are members of the EAPC Reference Group for Family Carers.

TS: Researching new horizons for integrated, community-oriented health systems
data.description:
Research into Primary Care.

This dynamic and participatory session builds on recent global discussions and research around community-oriented primary palliative care, highlighting as care shifts to community settings, integration of palliative care within primary care is more essential. The first presentation will share new international data on compassionate community interventions and outcomes. The second will explore implementation and evaluation of interventions in primary palliative care, focusing on equity, continuity, and measurable outcomes. The final speaker will present an emerging conceptual definition of primary palliative care as a bridge across systems, communities, and care providers. An interactive segment will follow, inviting delegates to co-create components of a shared definition using tools such as digital boards and word clouds. This collaborative process aims to advance a more inclusive and globally resonant framework for primary palliative care, aligned with WHO’s vision for universal health coverage. The session brings together researchers and practitioners from across continents and disciplines.

Aims and learning objectives:

This session explores innovative pathways to integrate palliative care within primary health systems, emphasising community-oriented care, measurable outcomes, and global equity. Participants will:

• Examine global data and indicators essential for evaluating compassionate community models.

• Reflect how palliative care can best be recognised, valued, and measured in primary care

• Understand a broader conceptualisation of primary palliative care

• Engage in proposing a new research and policy agenda that integrates community capacity, informal networks, and lay caregiving into mainstream palliative care strategies and indicators

data.title: Transforming Clinician Practice Through Interactive Palliative Care Education: Lessons from the EPEC Model
data.description: This session is sponsored by the Vlček Family Foundation: https://nrv.org/

schedule_event_manual_content.title: Transforming Clinician Practice Through Interactive Palliative Care Education: Lessons from the EPEC Model
schedule_event_manual_content.presenter_biography: Elisa and Mark Stad Professor of Pediatric Pain Medicine, Palliative Care and Integrative Medicine at UCSF, where he serves as Chief of the Division and Medical Director of the Stad Center at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospitals. He leads one of the nation’s most comprehensive pediatric pain and palliative care programs, recognized by ChildKind International and The Joint Commission. A global educator and researcher, he has delivered over 900 lectures across six continents and published extensively in the field. Dr. Friedrichsdorf is the principal investigator of the NIH/NCI-funded multisite study on the creation, implementation and evaluation of the Pediatric Palliative Care Curriculum “Education in Palliative and End-of-Life Care (EPEC)-Pediatrics” (which trained 2,500 clinicians from 126 countries) and founder of the annual Pediatric Pain Master Class. In 2024, he was named one of Time Magazine’s “100 Most Influential People in Health.”
schedule_event_manual_content.summary:
Objectives:

  1. Identify limitations of traditional didactic approaches in Palliative Medicine education and why they often fail to produce meaningful behavior change among clinicians.
  2. Examine evidence-based interactive teaching strategies - including “Needs Assessment,” “One Thing,” “Hook,” “Attitudes/Myths/Barriers,” “Knowledge,” and “Skill” -that foster engagement and practical application.
  3. Demonstrate these strategies in action through the exemplar lecture “Addressing Hope at Times of Clinical Uncertainty: Goals of Care as a Core Palliative Intervention”, and analyze their impact on clinician behavior from a meta-teaching perspective.

Abstract:

Traditional lectures in Palliative Medicine often fall short of inspiring meaningful behavioral change among clinicians and subsequently fail to result in improving clinical care of patients. The Education in Palliative and End-of-Life Care (EPEC) model offers a transformative approach by integrating interactive strategies that engage learners on cognitive, emotional, and practical levels. This session explores why conventional teaching methods may fail and introduces proven techniques, including —Needs Assessment, One Thing, Hook, Attitudes/Myths/Barriers, Knowledge, and Skill—that drive lasting impact. Participants will examine how these strategies shift clinician attitudes, dismantle misconceptions, and build actionable competencies. The lecture will showcase an exemplar session, “Addressing Hope at Times of Clinical Uncertainty: Goals of Care as a Core Palliative Intervention” to illustrate how these methods are applied in real-world teaching in different settings. Attendees will engage in a meta-teaching analysis to understand how each strategy contributes to behavior change. By the end, educators will be equipped to design sessions that not only inform but transform clinical practice and improve care of patients with serious illness. This presentation invites medical educators to rethink their approach and embrace a model that aligns with the realities of adult learning. Join us to discover how interactive education can elevate palliative care delivery—one clinician at a time.

data.title: EAPC Groups: Palliative Sedation. Evidence, guidelines, and controversies
data.description:
Palliative sedation involves the intentional lowering of the level of consciousness in patients with life-limiting disease who are experiencing refractory suffering. There are many differences between European countries in its application and its use across palliative care practices. The session will start with explaining the main content of the updated framework on palliative sedation (published 2024), including some controversies. The session will continue with the main findings from a recent international multicenter study on palliative sedation (published 2024), showing a significant decrease of discomfort levels. The session will continue with experiences of relatives and healthcare professionals regarding palliative sedation (published 2025). Here, palliative sedation will be discussed as a complex intervention, with mixed experiences of relief and distress. Finally, the role of communication. Despite variations between settings, open dialogue with patients, families, and HCPs was considered valuable (publication 2025). The session will finish with space for discussion.

Attendees will learn which elements around palliative sedation reached expert consensus and which elements are still controversial in the debate surrounding palliative sedation, based on the updated framework for palliative sedation (published in 2024). In addition, highlights from European research will be shown regarding its medical aspects and the experiences of professionals and relatives. There will be space for a guided discussion.

Speakers:

1. Prof Dr Lukas Radbruch, University of Bonn, Germany

2. Prof Dr Jeroen Hasselaar, Radboudumc, the Netherlands 

3. Prof Dr Sheila Payne, Lancaster University, England

4. Dr Agnes Csikos, Pecs University, Hungary 


All speakers are members of the EAPC Task Force on Palliative Sedation.

TS: Integrating palliative care into respiratory care: Challenges, innovations, and European collaboration
data.description:
Research into the management of symptoms and patient and family needs.

This themed session will feature three interconnected presentations.

Ágnes Csikós (University of Pécs) will discuss the challenges of integrating palliative care into respiratory care, including barriers at the patient, provider, and system levels, highlighting complexities such as unpredictable disease trajectories and the management of breathlessness.

Nancy Preston (Lancaster University) will present the ICLEAR intervention developed by Dr Paul Marsden at the Royal Preston Hospital in the UK, which helped integrate palliative care and improved communication between teams, reduced hospital admissions and enabled people to spend more time at home toward the end of life.

Luc Deliens (Vrije Universiteit Brussel) will introduce the EU PAL-COPD project, a large-scale, stepped-wedge RCT adapting and scaling the ICLEAR intervention across Europe. We will share preliminary findings from the first control wedge.

The session will conclude with a panel discussion inviting audience questions and reflections on the speakers’ experiences implementing ICLEAR in their respective countries.

Aims and learning objectives:

This session will highlight the importance of integrating palliative care into respiratory services for patients with advanced respiratory diseases. Participants will: Recognise the challenges and barriers to effective integration; Learn from the practical experiences of a UK study embedding palliative care within respiratory clinics; Gain insights into the EU PAL-COPD project, a European initiative focused on integrated palliative care in COPD. By the end of the session, attendees will be able to critically assess implementation strategies and explore ways to improve patient-centred care in respiratory services across diverse healthcare settings.

data.title: EAPC Partnered Research: 'Ask the experts anything'
data.description:
Chaired by Jeroen Hasselaar and Geana Kurita

​This session will be promoted to delegates who are at the early stage of their palliative care research career and give them an opportunity to ‘ask the experts anything’. There would also be the opportunity to ask the delegates what they would like to see under the themes of research capacity building at future EAPC congresses which would support the renewed reference group to plan for this starting in Glasgow in 2027. Followed by a small drinks reception for attendees of the session and stream panellists.

data.title: EAPC Groups: Strong Foundations, Shaky Grounds: LGBT+ Palliative Care in a Polarized World
data.description:
This session focuses on the implementation of the EAPC’s LGBT+ palliative care guidelines across varying cultural and geopolitical contexts. Katherine Bristowe will outline current translation and adaptation efforts across Europe. Theodor Kruse will address the urgent and specific needs of trans communities under threat, highlighting the role of palliative care professionals in responding to crisis with advocacy and action. Max Kleijberg will ground the discussion in real-world examples from Sweden, exploring practical tools for healthcare teams to offer inclusive care. Together, these presentations offer insight into translating policy into practice, building intersectional care structures, and responding to an increasingly polarized world.

This session aims to explore how EAPC recommendations for LGBT+ inclusive palliative care are being translated into local contexts amid rising anti-LGBT+ sentiment. Participants will learn how to implement culturally sensitive and inclusive practices, especially for trans individuals facing systemic threats. The session also fosters critical reflection on the intersection of care, politics, and equity, offering practical tools and solidarity-driven frameworks for clinical, educational, and policy responses.

Speakers:

Dr Katherine Bristowe – King’s College London, UK
Theodor P. Kruse – Sygehus Lillebælt, Denmark
Max Kleijberg – Mälardalen University / Karolinska Institutet, Sweden

All speakers are members of the EAPC Task Force on Palliative Care for LGBT+ People

user.name: Katherine
user.biography: Katherine Bristowe is a sociolinguist and qualitative methodologist whose research focuses on widening access to palliative care and bereavement support for individuals from minoritised and marginalised groups, and improving communication in the context of advanced illness.
